name: CRGO Electrical Steel & Transformer Core Localisation
scope: India's import-dependent CRGO / amorphous transformer-steel supply chain, the DGTR anti-dumping probe, JSW JFE capacity build-out, and the listed steel makers, core processors and transformer makers exposed to it.

summary.one_line: India imports ~90% of its 400-450 kt/yr CRGO need while the only domestic maker, JSW Steel's 50:50 JV with JFE, has petitioned for anti-dumping duties and is building toward 350 ktpa from FY28. A duty would help the JV years before its capacity can cover demand, and would squeeze processors and transformer makers in the meantime.
key_points: Demand is about 400-450 kt a year against 40-50 kt of domestic output, so nearly 90% is imported (S1, S3). Imports of the products under investigation were worth $821.5m in FY26, up 15.5% YoY. China supplied 33.6% of the wider CRGO category, Japan 31.4%, Russia 20.6% and Korea 6.5% (S4).

DGTR opened the anti-dumping case on 22 Jun 2026 (F. No. 6/17/2026-DGTR, SETU AD/OI/016/2026). It covers CRGO and amorphous metal from China, Japan, Korea and Russia, on a petition by JSW JFE Electrical Steel Nashik (S5, S2). The period of investigation is Apr 2025-Mar 2026 (S1, S6). The applicant has asked for duties to apply retrospectively, up to 90 days before any provisional duty (S6).

By 3 Sep 2026, 98 interested-party entries had registered. User-industry or importer registrants include listed CG Power, Hitachi Energy India, Indo Tech Transformers, Transformers & Rectifiers India, Atlanta Electricals and BHEL. Mangal Electrical is the only listed name filed as a 'supporter to domestic industry' (S5).

JSW JFE plans to expand Nashik from 50 to 250 ktpa (about Rs 4,300 cr) and Vijayanagar from 62 to 100 ktpa (an extra Rs 1,545 cr). Total spend is Rs 5,845 cr, with phases commissioning from FY2028 to a total of 350 ktpa (S7, S8). Completion of the Nashik tunnel furnaces is targeted for Q1 2027 (S9).

GTRI argues a duty would raise transformer costs while domestic output still meets under one-tenth of demand. It notes imports already need BIS certification, so the dispute is about price, not quality (S1, S3). TERI estimates that a 10% rise in CRGO prices adds 1.5-3% to transformer cost (S11).

The listed processors are small and under margin pressure. Jay Bee's FY26 EBITDA margin fell to 6.2% from 11.7% as CRGO prices dropped 30-35% (S14). Vilas grew Q1 FY27 revenue 18.2% to Rs 132.4 cr even though CRGO prices fell about 20% to Rs 190-195/kg (S13).

The market has not re-rated the theme. Vilas was +15.6% over 6 months but -19.6% over 1 year as of 23 Sep 2026 (S18). Jay Bee was -64% over 1 year as of 17 Jun 2026 (S19). JSW Steel was +8.5% over 6 months and +6.0% over 1 year as of 7 Oct 2026 (S20). We found no broker initiation that frames any of these as a CRGO play.

for_investors.title: Who benefits
points: JSW Steel, through its 50:50 JSW JFE JV, is the only domestic CRGO producer and the petitioner (S3, S5). A duty would support pricing as Nashik and Vijayanagar ramp toward 350 ktpa from FY28 (S8).

Processors with domestic sourcing options. ICRA notes Vilas has diversified to domestic CRGO suppliers since FY2021 (S12). Mangal Electrical, a 16,200 MT CRGO processor, registered as a supporter of the domestic industry (S5, S22).
Proterial's Metglas amorphous plant at Sri City (about 30 kt/yr, JV with unlisted Shirdi Sai Electricals) would be local supply inside any duty wall (S16).

for_investors.title: Who is hurt / risks
points: Transformer makers that import CRGO: Indo Tech is registered as both user and importer, and TARIL as importer (S5). CRGO is about 33-35% of their raw-material cost, according to TARIL (S10).

Small processors take the price pass-through risk on thin margins. Jay Bee's FY26 PAT margin was 3.3% (S14). ICRA flags Vilas's exposure to CRGO price and availability, its 80-90 day inventory and its customer concentration of ~45-55% (S12).

For JSW Steel the payoff is small and late. The JV is unlisted and only 50% owned (S7). JSW Steel booked Rs 47,364 cr of revenue in Q1 FY27 alone (S21), and the expansion only starts commissioning from FY2028 (S8).

for_investors.title: What to watch
points: DGTR disclosure statement and final findings, then the Ministry of Finance decision on any duty (S24). No preliminary findings were public at the time of writing.
Whether the Nashik furnace hits its Q1 2027 completion target (S9), the Vijayanagar timeline (S8), and the start of Proterial's Sri City plant (S16).
H1/Q2 FY27 results from Vilas and Jay Bee: whether Vilas holds its 45-50% FY27 growth guidance (S13) and whether Jay Bee's working capital normalises (S14).

subsections.title: What CRGO and amorphous metal are

blocks.text: Cold-rolled grain-oriented (CRGO) electrical steel and amorphous metal are the core materials of power and distribution transformers. About 98% of CRGO output goes into transformers (S11). Amorphous ribbon, such as Proterial's Metglas, cuts transformer no-load losses and can reduce standby power use by roughly one-third compared with conventional electrical sheet (S16). In the case initiation, DGTR took a prima facie view that CRGO and amorphous metal are substitutable for transformer cores, which is why both are in scope even though the applicant makes only CRGO (S6).

The supply chain has three layers: steel mills that make CRGO coil; processors that slit, cut and assemble it into laminations and cores (Vilas, Jay Bee, Mangal, TARIL's POSCO Poggenamp unit); and transformer makers (S10, S12, S22). Sources disagree on CRGO's cost share because they measure it on different bases. TARIL puts it at about 33-35% of transformer raw-material cost (S10). TERI puts it at 15-20% of a standard transformer's bill of materials, while an MSME source quoted 40-50% (S11).

blocks.text: GTRI raises a methodology objection. DGTR treated China as a non-market economy and, citing a lack of domestic price data for Japan, Korea and Russia, largely used the Indian producer's cost as the benchmark for all four countries (S3). GTRI also notes that CRGO was previously left out of safeguard duties because of continued import dependence (S1). The Indian Steel Association counters that CRGO needs 7-10 times the investment per tonne of conventional greenfield steel, and that unchecked subsidised imports could undermine foreign investor confidence (S11).

Opposition is broad. DGTR's 3 Sep 2026 list contains 98 interested-party entries, including the Embassy of Japan, the Russian Ministry of Economic Development, IEEMA, KOSA and the China Iron and Steel Association. Several listed transformer makers registered as user industry or importers (S5).

blocks.text: Our arithmetic: even with the full 350 ktpa from the JV and 30 kt of amorphous ribbon, announced capacity of about 380 kt would sit below today's 400-450 kt demand estimate (S1, S8, S16). The grid plan more than doubles transformer capacity, from 1,290 GVA in 2024 to 2,342 GVA by 2032 (S11). Imports therefore look set to remain the marginal source of supply through at least FY28-30.

blocks.text: Falling CRGO prices have so far hurt the processors more than any duty could. Jay Bee's CRGO volume rose about 25% in FY26, but CRGO revenue grew only about 10% as realisations fell, after raw-material prices dropped 30-35% between Mar 2025 and Mar 2026 (S14). Vilas's Q1 FY27 revenue rose despite CRGO prices falling about 20% to Rs 190-195/kg (S13). A duty would reverse that price trend. Processors that can pass costs through would see inventory gains; any lag in pass-through would compress margins that ICRA already flags as sensitive to CRGO prices and forex, with no formal hedging (S12). Neither Vilas nor Jay Bee appears on DGTR's interested-party list (S5).

JSW Steel holds 50% of the JV; JFE holds the other half (S7). For scale, JSW Steel reported Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue of Rs 47,364 cr (S21). As an illustration only (our arithmetic, not a forecast): 350 ktpa at the Rs 190-195/kg CRGO price Vilas cites (S13) gives roughly Rs 6,700 cr of gross revenue for the whole JV. That is under 4% of JSW Steel's annualised Q1 revenue even before applying JSW's 50% share, and not before FY28-30.

Downstream, the DGTR registrants include CG Power (registered as both user industry and exporter/producer), Hitachi Energy India, Indo Tech (user and importer), TARIL (importer), Atlanta Electricals and BHEL (S5). TARIL has partly hedged through backward integration: in Jan 2025 it bought 51% of POSCO Poggenamp Electrical Steel, a 24,000 t/yr CRGO processor (S10).

items: GTRI (Ajay Srivastava): a duty raises transformer and grid costs while giving only limited protection, because domestic output is under one-tenth of demand. He calls the four-country common Indian cost benchmark questionable (S1, S3).
TERI (Alekhya Datta): a 10% rise in CRGO prices adds 1.5-3% to transformer cost and a 20% rise adds 3-6%. Tariff effects would be gradual because capex is recovered over the asset's life (S11).
Indian Steel Association (Alok Sahay): domestic CRGO capacity is capital-intensive, and subsidised imports threaten investment (S11).
An MSME federation official, speaking anonymously, says JSW is 'the only beneficiary' of the probe in an MSME-dominated sector (S11).

ICRA (Vilas, Jul 2025): reaffirmed [ICRA]A- (Stable)/A2+. It cites strong debt metrics (interest cover 29.7x) against working-capital intensity, customer concentration and exposure to CRGO prices (S12).

blocks.text: Coverage is thin. We found no sell-side initiation or sector note that frames JSW Steel, Vilas or Jay Bee as a CRGO localisation play. Discussion is limited to think tanks, trade press, a rating rationale, and retail-oriented analysis sites such as multibagg.ai (S14). This is consistent with a theme that is still undiscovered.

subsections.title: Has the market priced it in?

blocks.caption: Stock performance (latest dated readings found; see dashboard for today's numbers)

blocks.text: Neither processor has re-rated on the probe. Vilas's 52-week range was Rs 313-535 as of 23 Sep 2026 (S18). Jay Bee's de-rating tracks its FY26 earnings decline, with PAT down from Rs 25.4 cr to Rs 18.3 cr (S14, S19).

items: The duty could be rejected or diluted. Opposition is organised, including foreign governments, industry associations and large user-industry registrants (S5), and GTRI and TERI point to the cost to the grid (S1, S11).
Commissioning could slip. New JV capacity starts only from FY2028 (S8), so a duty imposed in 2027 would raise costs before domestic supply is available.
Processors face price volatility. CRGO prices fell 30-35% in FY26 and cut Jay Bee's EBITDA margin roughly in half (S14). A duty-led rebound could squeeze processors that cannot pass it through (S12).
Liquidity and concentration: both processors are small caps (see dashboard for market caps), and Vilas depends on one customer for ~45-55% of sales (S12).
Materiality for JSW Steel: the JV is unlisted and 50%-owned, and small relative to group revenue (S7, S21).

companies.name: JSW Steel
companies.role: Owns 50% of JSW JFE Electrical Steel, India's only CRGO producer (Nashik, 50 ktpa), which is expanding to 350 ktpa (S3, S7, S8).
companies.impact: Its JV is the petitioner and main beneficiary of any duty (S5, S11), but CRGO is small next to JSW Steel's Rs 47,364 cr quarterly revenue and is ramping only from FY2028 (S8, S21).

companies.name: Vilas Transcore
companies.role: Vadodara maker of CRGO laminations and slit, stacked, wound and toroidal cores, with 36,000 MTPA capacity (S12, S13).
companies.impact: Volume grew 41% in Q1 FY27 despite ~20% lower CRGO prices (S13). Imports a significant share of its CRGO, with 80-90 days of inventory and no formal hedging, so a duty-led price swing hits margins (S12).

companies.name: Jay Bee Laminations
companies.role: CRGO core and lamination processor (23,340 MTPA), also making transformers and doing EPC work (S14, S15).
companies.impact: FY26 EBITDA margin fell to 6.2% on CRGO price swings and receivables more than doubled (S14). The stock was down ~64% over 1 year as of Jun 2026 (S19).

companies.name: Mangal Electrical Industries
companies.role: Rajasthan CRGO processor with 16,200 MT capacity plus transformers and 2,400 MT of amorphous units; listed Aug 2025 (S22).
companies.impact: The only listed company registered with DGTR as a 'supporter to domestic industry' in the CRGO case (S5).

companies.name: Transformers & Rectifiers (India)
companies.role: Power transformer maker that owns 51% of POSCO Poggenamp, a 24,000 t/yr CRGO processor (S10).
companies.impact: Registered with DGTR as an importer (S5). CRGO is 33-35% of its raw-material cost, so a duty raises input costs (S10).

companies.name: Indo Tech Transformers
companies.role: Transformer maker registered as both user industry and importer of CRGO in the DGTR case (S5).
companies.impact: Exposed to higher CRGO costs if a duty is imposed; TERI puts the hit at 1.5-3% of transformer cost per 10% rise in CRGO prices (S11).

companies.name: CG Power and Industrial Solutions
companies.role: Transformer maker registered with DGTR as both user industry and exporter/producer (S5).
companies.impact: A large CRGO consumer opposing or engaging in the case; a duty raises input costs (S5, S11).

companies.name: Hitachi Energy India
companies.role: Power transformer maker registered as user industry in the CRGO probe (S5).
companies.impact: Exposed to CRGO cost inflation. The grid plan to 2,342 GVA by 2032 supports demand (S1, S5).

companies.name: Atlanta Electricals
companies.role: Power and inverter-duty transformer maker listed Sep 2025, with 94,000 MVA supplied as of Mar 2025 (S23); registered as user industry (S5).
companies.impact: A CRGO buyer, so a duty raises input costs (S5, S11).

companies.name: Bharat Heavy Electricals
companies.role: State-owned transformer and power-equipment maker registered in the probe as user industry and government (S5).
companies.impact: A CRGO consumer affected by any duty (S5).

method: First edition, researched 24-25 Oct 2026 with web search and direct page fetches. Primary anchors are the DGTR interested-party notice for case 6/17/2026-DGTR (read in full), the ICRA rating rationale for Vilas Transcore (read in full), and company NSE filings, whose figures were taken from search-result extracts because the PDFs timed out. GTRI, TERI and ISA views come from trade-press reports. Capex and capacity figures come from coverage of JSW Steel's Aug 2025 exchange filing. Stock returns are the latest dated third-party readings we found, so dates differ by stock; today's figures are on the dashboard (numbers.json). Dates for S16 (publication month known, day approximated), S21 and S24 (approximate publication dates) are best estimates; source IDs skip S17. Sources disagree on CRGO's share of transformer cost and on the injury period; both versions are shown. We found no DGTR preliminary findings or sell-side notes on the theme, so none are reported. Other listed names come from DGTR's registrant list and from processor IPO and acquisition disclosures. We found no listed mid-cap CRGO steel maker other than JSW Steel's JV. Voltamp and Shilchar were left out because we found no dated, citable source tying them to CRGO. Shirdi Sai Electricals (Metglas JV partner) appears to be unlisted. Illustrative revenue arithmetic is our own and labelled as such; no ratings or price targets are given.

electrical_steel_makers: Listed companies making or building CRGO / amorphous electrical steel capacity, directly or through a JV
core_processors: Listed companies slitting, cutting and assembling CRGO into transformer laminations and cores, expanding capacity
